plan.topic: GLP-1 medicines and anaesthesia: regurgitation or aspiration in 1.41% of GLP-1 users vs 0.12% of non-users (UK prospective observational cohort, 47,039 patients, 119 sites, Anaesthesia)
plan.angle: Title: 'GLP-1 Meds Like Semaglutide & Anesthesia: 1.41% vs 0.12% in UK Study #shorts' (or 'Taking Semaglutide or Tirzepatide Before Surgery? What a UK Study Found'). First line: 'On a GLP-1 medicine like semaglutide or tirzepatide and having surgery or an endoscopy? Tell your anaesthetist.' Mechanism: slower stomach emptying can leave food in the stomach. Numbers: among 1,348 people who had used a GLP-1 medicine in the previous 3 months, 19 had regurgitation or aspiration (17 regurgitation, 2 aspiration): 1.41%, vs 0.12% of everyone else (about 1 in 71 vs 1 in 802). On-screen: 'observational · linked to, not proof · UK hospitals · GLP-1 users were more likely to have obesity/diabetes'. Guidance: 'Professional guidance differs, so your surgical team decides the plan.' Only action: tell your surgical and anaesthesia team and follow their instructions. Never say stop, pause or keep taking it on your own. Close with: 'It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.' 35–50s.
plan.working_title: Semaglutide (Ozempic) & Anesthesia: 1.41% vs 0.12% Regurgitation in UK Study #shorts
plan.why: A high-intent search ('stop Ozempic before surgery') with a fresh prospective study. The radar marked it caution, so the angle is limited to 'tell your team', which is safe and genuinely useful. | fact-check: Verified: Potter TE et al., 'Peri-operative glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist use and outcomes: a national prospective multicentre cohort study', Anaesthesia 2026. 47,039 patients, 119 UK sites, 1,348 GLP-1 RA users (2.9%). 19 events (17 regurgitation, 2 aspiration) = 1.41% vs 57/45,691 = 0.12% (OR 11.39; about 1 in 71 vs 1 in 802). GLP-1 use was defined as use within 3 months before the procedure. The authors say causality can't be determined: obesity and diabetes, both aspiration risk factors, were more common in the GLP-1 group, and events may have been under-reported. That confounding caveat must be on screen or in the narration. The Association of Anaesthetists recommends continuing GLP-1 RAs peri-operatively, while other societies' guidance has differed, so the 'your team decides' framing is right. Never tell viewers to stop, pause or continue on their own. Title problem: the study covered all GLP-1 RAs, not semaglutide or Ozempic specifically. Leading with 'Semaglutide (Ozempic)' implies a drug-specific result the study didn't report. Name the class first, with examples.

social.instagram_caption:
Having surgery or an endoscopy soon? If you're on a GLP-1 medicine, this matters. 🩺

A UK study tracked 47,039 patients across 119 hospitals.

Regurgitation or aspiration under anesthesia happened in 1.41% of recent GLP-1 users vs 0.12% of everyone else — roughly 1 in 71 vs 1 in 802.

GLP-1s (semaglutide, tirzepatide) slow stomach emptying, so food can linger longer than expected before a procedure.

The catch: this is observational. GLP-1 users in the study were also more likely to have obesity or diabetes, which raise aspiration risk on their own, and the study didn't adjust for that. Some events may have gone unreported too. Professional guidance still differs, so your surgical team makes the final call. Tell them you're on it and follow their instructions.

Save this as a reminder to tell your surgical team you're on a GLP-1 before your next procedure.

factcheck.summary:
I checked the cited study (Potter TE et al., the GLIMPSE study, Anaesthesia 2026, DOI 10.1111/anae.70380) against the Association of Anaesthetists press release on EurekAlert and MedicalXpress coverage. Every number in the script matches:
- 47,039 patients at 119 UK sites.
- 1,348 GLP-1 users, screened for use in the 3 months before the procedure.
- 19 events in that group: 17 regurgitation and 2 aspiration (1.41%).
- 0.12% in the 45,691 non-users (57 events).
- The derived figures are right: 1 in 71 and 1 in 802.

The framing is sound. The script calls the study observational, gives the absolute figures next to the relative gap, and names the confounding by obesity and diabetes that the authors themselves raise. Safety is handled well: there is no advice to stop the drug or about fasting, and the plan is left to the surgical team. That fits the Association of Anaesthetists' position, which is to continue the medicine and tell the team. The prescriber line is present.

There are four minor fixes:
- Swap the PubMed search URL for the paper's DOI link.
- Name the outcome in the title.
- Add a short note that the study did not adjust for obesity or diabetes.
- Add a small caveat on scope about endoscopy.

issues.problem: This is a PubMed search-results URL, not a link to the paper. The source list needs a stable, direct URL.
issues.fix: Replace the url with "https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.70380" and set the publisher to "Anaesthesia (Association of Anaesthetists / Wiley), Potter TE et al. (GLIMPSE study)".

issues.claim: GLP-1 Meds Like Semaglutide & Anesthesia: 1.41% vs 0.12% in UK Study #shorts
issues.problem: The title gives the numbers without saying what they measure. The craft rules say to name the outcome and not tease bare numbers, and the observational hedge is missing.
issues.fix: Semaglutide & Other GLP-1s Before Anesthesia: Regurgitation 1.41% vs 0.12% in UK Study #shorts

issues.claim: GLP-1 users were more likely to have obesity or diabetes, both aspiration risks themselves, and events may have been under-reported.
issues.problem: The script is accurate, but it leaves out that the study did not adjust for these confounders. The authors also said under-reporting may have affected events in the non-GLP-1 group, which bears on how large the gap really is.
issues.fix: Here's the catch. It's observational: linked to, not proof. GLP-1 users were more likely to have obesity or diabetes, both aspiration risks themselves, and the study didn't adjust for them. Some events may also have gone unreported.

issues.claim: booked for surgery or an endoscopy? Tell your anesthesia team.
issues.problem: The study covered procedures under the care of an anaesthetist; the sources I checked don't confirm whether sedation-only endoscopy was included. Telling the team before an endoscopy is still reasonable, consistent advice. The script just shouldn't imply that the 1.41% figure applies specifically to endoscopy.
issues.fix: No narration change is needed. Keep the s3 attribution exactly as "119 UK hospitals · observational", and don't add endoscopy-specific wording to the s3 or s4 stat labels or to the captions.

notes: The small 'Stomach' label pill overlaps the lower caption text ('how fast your stomach empties') per the layout audit at 11.77s.
The floating body outline with the stomach leaves large empty purple areas top and bottom — sparse composition for a multi-second shot.
The small black 'Stomach' pill text is tiny against the purple background, likely under 40px.

Both frames (14.0s and 16.9s) are essentially a bare body outline with a small stomach or lungs icon and an arrow on a plain purple gradient — well under the ~25% hero-art coverage guideline, with no headline for several seconds.

Caption spells numbers as words ('FOLLOWED FORTY-SEVEN THOUSAND', 'AND NINETEEN HOSPITALS') while the stat card above shows numerals ('47,039', '119 UK hospitals') — this breaks the numerals-must-match-the-pill rule and 'AND NINETEEN' reads like '19' instead of '119', which is actively misleading.
The number is split across two caption screens in a way that could be misread mid-value.
The '19 of 1,348 users' pill sits directly on top of the hero artwork (people/stomach) at both 27.3s and 32.2s, per the layout audit.
Caption spells the number out as words across two overlapping lines ('Of the one thousand, / three hundred and forty-eight'), which collides with other on-screen text and is unreadable at a glance.
Second caption uses 'NINETEEN HAD REGURGITATION' instead of the numeral '19', inconsistent with the pill.
The caption 'FOUR ONE PERCENT,' overlaps other on-screen text per the audit (35.27s) and reads ambiguously instead of '1.41%'.
The following orphan fragment 'PERCENT OF EVERYONE ELSE.' doesn't restate the number, so a viewer who missed the stat card can't tell what percent is being compared.

Caption 'VERSUS ONE IN EIGHT' contradicts the stat card shown just before it ('About 1 in 71 vs 1 in 802') — '1 in 802' appears to have been truncated into 'one in eight', which is a factual error on screen, not just a typography issue.
A single magnifying-glass icon is held alone on a plain teal gradient for about 3 seconds (45.9–48.8s), with large empty space around it — violates the no-lone-icon-on-plain-gradient rule.
Two small icon circles (body shape, pointing hand) float on a plain background with a lot of dead space; composition feels sparse for two consecutive caption beats.
Captions 'GLP-1 USERS WERE' and 'THE STUDY DIDN'T' are orphaned sentence fragments that don't read as a complete thought on their own.

audio.soundNotes: Music sat a touch hot in pauses (-11.2 dB vs a ~-14 target) while under-speech level was already on-target, so I applied a single -2 dB (0.8×) trim that keeps speech-bed music in range and pulls pause swells closer to target without starving it under narration. SFX cleanup focused on three over-dense clusters (the ~8.3–9.5s mechanism reveal, the ~26.2s stat pop, and the ~60.4–61.5s "some may be missed" transition) where 5–7 cues were stacked in about a second — trimmed each to 3–4 by dropping redundant bubbles/swooshes and one loud bubble that was sitting at -4.2 dB over the voice. Also tamed a couple of stray speech-bed cues that read louder than the -14 to -20 dB window (a swoosh at -10.6 dB, a blip at -13.7 dB) and dropped a near-silent swell cue that was adding nothing. Added four bespoke, low-level accents (opening monitor ping, a tense pulse under the risk stats, a reflective chime at the "linked to, not proof" turn, and a warm bell swell going into the prescriber CTA) to mark the story's emotional beats without ever competing with the narration.

approved_by: editor-in-chief (low risk): The hold was for a 5% subtitle mismatch, and every flagged diff is a transcription quirk, not a real mismatch: "&" heard as "and", "1.41" and "0.12" read out digit by digit, and "a" heard for "one". The final audio WER is 0.026.
